description: Echo can only repeat. Narcissus loves nothing but his reflection. Two fates that never manage to meet, and that gave us the word narcissism.

hero.hook: She has no voice of her own. He has eyes only for himself. Their meeting is impossible.

blocks.text: The Roman poet [[Ovid]] tells the crossed fates of **Narcissus** and **Echo** in his [[Metamorphoses]]. She is a nymph robbed of her own speech. He is a young man captivated by his own image.
This myth is the direct source of the word **narcissism**. It is about impossible love, indifference, and the trap of wanting nothing but yourself.

Before she became a simple sound effect, **Echo** was an [[Oread]], a mountain nymph famous for how much she talked. She helped **Zeus**, king of the gods, cover up his affairs. While he slipped away to other nymphs, she held **Hera**, his jealous wife, in endless conversation.

blocks.caption: Echo, condemned to be nothing but a voice that repeats

blocks.text: When Hera discovered the trick, she punished Echo. The nymph could no longer start a sentence. She could only **repeat the last words** spoken by someone else. Her own desires had no tongue left.
In another version, the god **Pan**, furious at being turned down, has Echo torn to pieces. Ovid's version, where she wastes away from love, stayed the most famous.

**Narcissus** was the son of the river god Cephissus and the nymph Liriope. His beauty drew everyone in. His pride pushed everyone away. The seer **Tiresias** had warned his mother: “He will live to be old if he never knows himself.”

In the woods, Echo saw him and fell in love. Unable to speak first, she waited. Narcissus called out: “Is anyone here?” She answered: “Here!” When she came closer to embrace him, he pushed her away with contempt.
Humiliated, Echo withdrew into the caves. She stopped eating. Her body dried up and her bones turned to stone. Nothing was left but a voice wandering in the mountains.

The cruelty of Narcissus wore the gods out. One of his victims prayed to [[Nemesis]], goddess of righteous vengeance: let him love himself the same way and never possess what he loves. The wish was granted.

On a hot day, Narcissus leaned over a clear spring. He saw his own face. He thought he was looking at a water spirit. He fell in love with it. The prophecy of Tiresias came true: by knowing himself, he lost himself.
He tried to kiss the reflection. The water clouded over. Trapped in that sterile passion, he forgot to eat and drink.
Then came the tragic clarity: “I am the one I see.” You cannot join with your own reflection. Narcissus wasted away. Echo, loyal in spite of everything, repeated his last farewell.

When the [[Naiads]], nymphs of the waters, and the [[Dryads]], nymphs of the trees, came for the funeral, the body was gone. In its place grew a flower with a yellow heart and white petals: the **narcissus**, leaning over the water like the young man over his image.

In **1914**, **Freud** published “On Narcissism: An Introduction”. In it he described love turned toward the self instead of toward another person. The myth became a key to modern psychology, and a warning: without a real meeting, all that is left is a voice without a body and a flower without a soul.
**Echo** died because she could not speak her desire. **Narcissus** died because he desired nobody but himself. Two ways of missing the other person, one single tragedy.
